connector: Chapter 15 ended with the Civil War beginning. Harriet watched soldiers march off singing “John Brown’s Body” and decided she would join the Union Army somehow. In Chapter 16 she sails south. Notice which moments Sterling gives whole pages to, and which get one line.

a.raw: the ship sailed slowly up the river harriet watched more closely than the lieutenant
a.fixed: The ship sailed slowly up the river. Harriet watched more closely than the lieutenant.
a.why: Capital T starts the sentence; a period ends the first sentence; capital H on Harriet. Slowly is a plain adverb; more closely compares how two people watched.

b.raw: general hunter paced faster as he talked harriet listened more carefully than ever
b.fixed: General Hunter paced faster as he talked. Harriet listened more carefully than ever.
b.why: Capital G and H on General Hunter (a title with a name); a period ends the first sentence; capital H on Harriet. Faster and more carefully are comparative adverbs.

scholar.journal-q1: … and tell which job Harriet seems to care about most.
scholar.journal-q2: … and use one thing the General says.
scholar.journal-q3: … and name one thing Sterling keeps short or leaves out.

fill1.h1: An elevator lifts you up to a higher floor. Which root means lift?
fill1.why: lev means lift: e + lev + ate = lift up.

fill2.h1: A lever is a bar you push down to lift something heavy. Which root means lift?
fill2.why: lev means lift: lev + er = a tool for lifting.

fill3.h1: When you stand against something and won’t give in, which root means stand?
fill3.why: sist means stand: re + sist = stand against.

fill4.h1: To keep standing through hard times and never quit. Which root means stand?
fill4.why: sist means stand: per + sist = stand through, keep going.

notes.wgrd: An author also shows her perspective by what she puts in and what she leaves out. The moments she spends whole pages on are the moments she thinks matter most.
vocab: To lift up; to raise to a higher level.
To stand against; to refuse to give in.
To keep going; to refuse to stop.
A person who worked to end (abolish) slavery.
notes.wordParts: lev means “lift” and sist means “stand”: elevate, lever, resist, persist.
notes.grammar: A comparative adjective describes a noun (a faster horse). A comparative adverb describes a verb (the horse ran faster). Ask what each comparing word describes.
notes.spelling: In a long word, one syllable gets the stress and is said loud and clear. A vowel in a quiet syllable often fades to a lazy “uh,” the schwa: ab·o·LI·tion. To spell it, find a related word where that syllable is stressed: a·BOL·ish.

catcher.intro: As you read Ch. 16, sort the moments.

end.label: What the long parts tell me Sterling cares about

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: lifting, or standing?

why.t: At the end of Chapter 16, in the camp outside Beaufort, a woman pieces together an American flag from scraps of old clothing and says, “Our time is coming.” lev means lift, and sist means stand. Each right word sews one patch. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. lev = lift, sist = stand.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. The Civil War has started, and Harriet won’t sit it out. Chapter 16 takes her south to Beaufort, South Carolina, where thousands of people have just escaped to the Union army. Today’s question: what can Harriet do there that nobody else can?
transcripts.read: Notice where Sterling spends her pages. Some moments get a whole page, and some get one line. Watch Harriet’s talk with General Hunter, and listen for a story about a snake. Then walk the camp at night with her. On my tours, people always ask about the book those kids were reading.
transcripts.grammar: Faster can describe a horse, or it can describe how the horse runs. When it describes a thing, it’s an adjective. When it tells how someone did something, it’s an adverb. So don’t just spot the comparing words. Ask what each one is describing.

virtue.title: Moving freedom forward?
virtue.intro: In Chapter 16, thousands of people have escaped to the Union army in Beaufort. Read each moment. Tap Moving freedom forward or Holding it back.

items.t: Mr. Lincoln won’t let escaped slaves join the army. He is afraid of losing Maryland and Kentucky.
items.why: While he waits, the people in Beaufort are called contrabands of war, not free men.

items.t: General Hunter forms the First South Carolina regiment from freed men.
items.why: Men who were enslaved now drill as soldiers, ready to fight for freedom.

items.t: By the firelight, a woman slowly spells aloud, “Cat, bat, pat.”
items.why: Learning to read is a freedom slavery tried to keep from her.

items.t: The soldiers are promised pay like the white soldiers, but the money never comes.
items.why: Without pay, a soldier with hungry children is only ‘half free.’

items.t: Harriet tells the General the war can’t be won by half measures.
items.why: She is pushing the Union to set the slaves free.

virtue.name: freedom
